blocks.p: The square of washi sat on the tatami where Rei had put it down at dawn, and for three hours of bad sleep he had not let himself touch it.

When he woke the light had gone the flat grey of a typhoon sky that never quite arrives. The cicadas had stopped. Somewhere down the street someone was testing a drum for the night, two beats and a pause, two beats and a pause. Rei sat up on the futon and looked at the paper and thought, very clearly, if this is from the Healer I will know the moment I open it. Then he opened it.

It was not from the Healer. He knew that before the last fold came undone, because the paper did not feel kind. It felt careful. Inside, in fine brush strokes the colour of weak tea, was a small dense figure he recognised from the dictionary he had read the morning before. Number six in Gin's list. The Stability Mark. Pressed to the inside of the wrist, it would hold a person's floor for one scene. It could be made for someone else, on their skin, at the maker's cost.
In the corner, small, was the letter again. R. And under it a date from June, before the handwriting leaned.

Gin had drawn it for him weeks before he went quiet. Gin had carried it in the cardigan pocket all month, under the Healer's nose, and at the foot of the stairs at dawn he had surfaced just far enough to put it in Rei's hand. Rei sat with it on his knee for a long time. Then he folded it again along its own creases and put it in his shirt pocket, over his heart, and got up to do the thing he had been putting off since the river.

blocks.cap: Three pages laid out side by side

blocks.p: He cleared the low table and then the floor beneath it, because the table was not large enough. He laid the three things down corner to corner on the tatami the way a man lays out the clothes of someone who is not coming back. Carefully. So the creases fell right, as though neatness could still do them any good.

The registry page first, the one the bookseller's locked shelf had finally given up, with the Thirteen ruled into it and the thirteenth line empty except for a date. Then the smallest of the bookseller's own notes, written in the cramped hand a man uses only when he is afraid of his own paper, about how the wall over Kita would thin on these nights and what it would look like when it did. Last, because he could not make his hand go any faster, a page of Gin's handwriting from after the fourteenth. The entry where the loops first leaned a degree the wrong way. He had read it so often that the fold had gone soft as cloth.

For a month he had carried all of it as one thing. A countdown. A single dread ticking toward one last night. That was how the Healer wanted it carried, light enough to run with, simple enough to panic over. Read your clocks, it had said. Plural. It had not been careless. It had been telling him.

On the floor, laid flat in the grey light, the dread came apart in his hands the way a chord comes apart when the ear finally hears the separate notes inside it. There was not one clock. There were three. And the quiet mathematical horror of the three was that they were not running at the same speed. They would not all reach the bottom of the hour together. One of them would get there first.

He let his registers come halfway up. Only halfway, the way Kurosawa had taught him in the cold room, enough to read and not enough to be read. The flat took on the second grain it always had when he did this. Paper remembered being a tree. The dead leaned closer to anything that was paying attention. Under that grain the three pages stopped being documents and became what they had been all along. Schedules.
He started with the wall, because it was the honest one, and honesty was the only mercy in the room.

Higuchi had written it in the hand of a man who had measured the thing he was describing and wished he had not. The membrane over Kita did not fail all at once and it did not fail forever. It thinned at Obon the way ice thins over a warm spring. It opened along the river through the festival's last nights. Then, at the first true light after the sending fires, it either closed back to its old hard quiet, or, if something had been driven through it while it was soft, it tore along the line of the wound and did not close at all.

doc.title: Higuchi's note, in letters barely a millimetre tall
lines: Last night of the festival. Okuribi. The ice is softest from the lighting of the fires to first light.
If nothing is pushed through, it heals by itself by morning. It always has. It does not need us.
If something is pushed through while it is soft, it will not heal.
Whoever reads this should be someone who will leave it alone. I do not know who that is. I am locking it up.

blocks.p: There was a clean edge to it that the other two did not have. It opened tonight. It shut at dawn. Everything that was going to be decided about the wall would be decided in the dark between.

Rei read the small letters twice and felt the particular cold of a deadline that cannot be argued with. The vacancy could wait years. It had. Gin could be pleaded with. Rei had tried. But the wall did not negotiate. It was weather, it was tide. It was the one thing on the embankment that would happen exactly the same way if Rei and Gin and the Healer had never been born. That indifference was almost a comfort. There was at least one clock in this whole disaster that was not aimed at him on purpose.

Under his half-raised registers the page showed him the thing Higuchi had been too disciplined to write. The bookseller had measured the thinning, and then he had locked the shelf. A man does not lock a true measurement away from a careful reader unless he has guessed what a careful reader would do with it. He had guessed that someone would come who could feel both sides of the wall at once. And he had guessed that such a person, handed the exact hour the ice went soft, would be the perfect tool for saving the wall or finishing it.
The measurement was honest. The hand that recorded it had been afraid of Rei, specifically, reading it. Both things were true at the same time. That was the shape of the whole month.
The chair was the patient clock, and it frightened him in a different key.

The registry ruled the Thirteen into their columns. Twelve of the lines held names Rei had come to know that month as people, tired and weakening and holding. Watanabe going grey at the edges. Mori Takao white-knuckled at his boiler. Nakashima Yuna in her stairwell. Inoue Satoru who never stopped moving. Park Junho on his knees in a room behind a restaurant. The whole exhausted choir keeping the wall up by being something.

The thirteenth line was ruled like the others and held only a year. 2009. The year the lights went grey. Under it, in a second ink, Higuchi had added lines of his own. The ledger had been started by an exorcist whose name was nowhere in it. Higuchi kept it current.

doc.title: The registry, line XIII, with Higuchi's annotations
lines: The holder died. Nobody with the right aperture was present at the crossing, so the succession did not take.
The centre has carried it directly since. It cannot do so forever.
Kita has thinned since that year. After the eleventh of March 2011 it thinned faster.
The Division's instruments read this register as stillness and file it as null-emotive. It is not empty. It is full. It does not vary because it does not need to.
Who can sit it. A practitioner who carries more than one path and can hold one unchanging register without letting it turn into any of the other twelve.

blocks.p: Rei read the last line and did not move for a while. More than one path. One unchanging register. He thought of the kitchen table and a younger Gin teaching him how to be quiet, calling it a family habit, a trick for sleeping, the way it had been handed down to him. He thought of the grain in his own palms that the far shore had left there.

Years of nothing ran down that column, kept open by the plain bureaucratic fact that nobody had crossed it out. Rei had read enough of the bookseller's shelf to know what that meant. An empty seat is not a hole in the wall. It is a chair at the wall, and an empty chair is a question the wall keeps asking.

This clock had been running longest and moving slowest, and that was exactly why the Healer had been patient with it. A seat does not stay open. It waits, and waiting is not forgetting. It waits for the ones who can close it. Tonight, for the first time since the lights went grey, the two who could close it would both be standing in the city while the ice was soft.

The chair had no dawn line. It was older and quieter than dawn. But it had a condition. The condition was met when a thing of the right register reached the right place at the moment the wall could be written on. So the patient clock had no hour of its own. It borrowed the wall's hour. That was the trap folded inside the registry, and the reason the page had been locked away. The patient clock and the honest clock would arrive together, tonight, at the seam, by design.

He held the page to the lamp and let his registers come the rest of the way to halfway, and he could almost feel the chair from the flat. Not a figure of speech. A real cold spot over the river in the shape of an absence. A pressure like a breath that had been held for six years and was, very slightly, beginning to let go.

The Healer wanted the seat. Rei had known that for days. What the registry told him that the Healer's reasonable voice never had was what the seat wanted. It wanted to be filled by whoever was standing in front of it when the wall went soft. It was not loyal to the Healer. It was not loyal to Rei. It was a chair, and a chair takes whoever sits.

And then something snagged, the way a thread snags on a nail. Rei frowned at the page. The centre has carried it directly since. The chair was not empty. It only read empty, because the one holding it was not alive to be counted. Somebody had been sitting in it for six years, on the far side of everything, with his back to the world.
The seat I became.
Rei set the registry down very carefully, as if it might go off. Then he reached for the third page, the one in his brother's hand, and turned it over.
